sources.note: Twelve observed intervals, twelve border files, state kind, imported summary and missing reviewed card.

sources.title: Human History Map imported summaries
sources.note: Current Wikipedia-derived copy reduces Shuar identity to hunting and tsantsa and requires replacement.

sources.title: Human History Map 1200 borders
sources.note: The exact target is absent immediately before its indexed beginning.

sources.title: Human History Map 1279 borders
sources.note: First exact seven-position polygon and the 1279 to 1300 interval.

sources.title: Human History Map 1300 borders
sources.note: The same component covers the 1300 to 1400 interval.

sources.title: Human History Map 1400 borders
sources.note: Minute coordinate drift begins the 1400 to 1492 interval without a meaningful territorial shift.

sources.title: Human History Map 1492 borders
sources.note: The exact id disappears for eight years and shuar-wampis owns the audited core and Gualaquiza.

sources.title: Human History Map 1500 borders
sources.note: The target returns with its former component for 1500 to 1530 while Inca owns audited western points.

sources.title: Human History Map 1530 borders
sources.note: A minimally shifted seven-point component covers 1530 to 1600.

sources.title: Human History Map 1600 borders
sources.note: The same target component continues for 1600 to 1650.

sources.title: Human History Map 1650 borders
sources.note: The target persists for 1650 to 1700 while outside audited points are assigned to the Viceroyalty of Peru.

sources.title: Human History Map 1700 borders
sources.note: Another hash change without meaningful extent change begins 1700 to 1715.

sources.title: Human History Map 1715 borders
sources.note: Target coverage continues while the atlas changes surrounding ownership from Peru to Spain.

sources.title: Human History Map 1783 borders
sources.note: Minute geometry drift begins the 1783 to 1800 interval.

sources.title: Human History Map 1800 borders
sources.note: The component persists from 1800 to 1815 with a changed geometry hash.

sources.title: Human History Map 1815 borders
sources.note: Last exact interval, 1815 to 1878; seven audited core points remain target-owned.

sources.title: Human History Map 1878 borders
sources.note: Target vanishes as Ecuador and Peru replace Indigenous layers at audited points.

sources.title: Two thousand years of garden urbanism in the Upper Amazon
sources.note: Science article combines lidar, excavation and survey to document much older Upano platforms, roads and fields without assigning them to Shuar.

sources.title: A 2,000-year-old urban network in Ecuadorian Amazonia
sources.note: French natural-history museum explains the Upano lidar discovery, dating and researchers’ cautious interpretation.

sources.title: Revista del Patrimonio Cultural del Ecuador 5
sources.note: Ecuadorian heritage journal presents archaeological work and regional context in Morona Santiago.

sources.title: LiDAR and “lost cities”: examining public presentation
sources.note: Peer-reviewed methods article warns that sensational media framing can outrun archaeological interpretation.

sources.title: Sangay National Park
sources.note: UNESCO describes eastern Andean to Amazon ecosystems, volcanism and rivers whose levels can change quickly.

sources.title: 501 bird species recorded in the Cordillera del Kutukú
sources.note: Ecuadorian biodiversity institute reports modern Shuar stewardship and exceptionally rich bird life; used only as living continuity.

sources.title: Tropical deforestation and Indigenous resistance over the longue durée in South America
sources.note: Peer-reviewed synthesis places Spanish mining incursions, mission attempts and Indigenous resistance in long environmental history.

sources.title: A Chronicle of Deception
sources.note: Archival synthesis details sixteenth- and seventeenth-century mines, forced labor, epidemics, uprisings, invasions and captives.

sources.title: Colonialism and resistance in the Amazon
sources.note: Science Panel for the Amazon chapter surveys colonial incursions and resistance, including the 1579 to 1608 eastern Ecuador frontier.

sources.title: La cultura material Shuar en los siglos XVI al XIX
sources.note: FLACSO repository record for a historical study of Shuar objects and changing material life from the sixteenth to nineteenth centuries.

sources.title: Jesuit missions in Maynas, 1638 to 1767
sources.note: Peer-reviewed mission history locates colonial evangelization, movement and conflict in the wider upper-Amazon borderlands.

sources.title: The Shuar and the Ecuadorian state, 1822 to 2010
sources.note: Historical synthesis discusses nineteenth-century trade paths, settlement, tools, cloth and changing relations with republican authorities.

sources.title: Extractive economies in Ecuadorian Amazonia
sources.note: FLACSO study traces late nineteenth-century quinine and rubber networks and exchanges involving firearms and manufactured goods.

sources.title: Relations and tensions in Salesian colonizing-mission projects
sources.note: Universidad Politécnica Salesiana research examines late nineteenth-century mission projects and Indigenous negotiation.

sources.title: Trade goods and Jívaro warfare: the Shuar 1850 to 1957
sources.note: Historical anthropology links trade goods, guns, frontier demand and changing warfare; the title preserves a dated exonym.

sources.title: Shuar migrants and Shrunken heads face to face in a zone of state intervention
sources.note: Anthropological analysis distinguishes household-centered histories, modern identity politics and state intervention.

sources.title: La conversión de los Shuar
sources.note: FLACSO journal article examines missionization, Indigenous agency and the later political federation.

sources.title: Shuar: political organization and federation
sources.note: Yale eHRAF ethnographic record helps date the federation to 1964 rather than projecting it backward.

sources.title: Community health research with Shuar communities
sources.note: Open peer-reviewed project describes contemporary community diversity, federation history and uneven market and healthcare access.

sources.title: Shuar language
sources.note: Glottolog identifies Shuar Chicham, ISO 639-3 jiv, alternate names and its Chicham-family classification.

sources.title: Fonología de las lenguas jívaras
sources.note: Linguistic study distinguishes Shuar, Achuar, Wampis and Awajún within the Chicham family while documenting sound systems.

sources.title: The Shuar writing boom
sources.note: Peer-reviewed study explains that sustained Shuar writing and a patrimonial written tradition are modern developments.

sources.title: Shuar Chicham publications
sources.note: FLACSO language archive lists modern grammars, dictionaries and recorded texts, not medieval manuscripts.

sources.title: Salesians and Shuar language documentation
sources.note: University repository study places missionary transcription, translation and schooling after the atlas interval.

sources.title: Shuar fieldsite: culture, cooperation and everyday life
sources.note: University fieldsite describes contemporary households, gardens, food sharing, fishing, chicha, music, education and healthcare for labeled comparison.

sources.title: Growing up Shuar
sources.note: Ethnographic research on contemporary childhood, learning, foods and household participation; used only as later comparison.

sources.title: Mammal hunting by the Shuar of the Ecuadorian Amazon
sources.note: Peer-reviewed modern study documents hunting routes, harvests and sustainability questions in one community.

sources.title: Wildlife-use research in Shuar communities
sources.note: Ecuadorian biodiversity conference research notes age and gender diversity in contemporary hunting; not an automatic historical rule.

sources.title: Shuar women and agrobiodiversity
sources.note: Scholarly study documents women’s contemporary agricultural knowledge in Miazi and Shaime for carefully labeled continuity.

sources.title: Work, sharing and inequality in Shuar communities
sources.note: Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute article examines contemporary cooperative work and changing inequality.

sources.title: La casa tradicional Shuar
sources.note: Peer-reviewed architectural study analyzes later traditional house form, symbolic zones and gendered space as comparison evidence.

sources.title: Cerámica Shuar: saberes y prácticas
sources.note: University of Cuenca repository preserves Shuar-authored knowledge about pottery making and intergenerational learning.

sources.title: Music of Ecuador
sources.note: Smithsonian Folkways catalogue includes recorded Shuar songs and performance as modern continuity, not a medieval soundtrack.

sources.title: Tsentsak: Shuar knowledge and healing
sources.note: Smithsonian catalog record identifies a Shuar-produced work based on interviews and community knowledge about healing specialists.

sources.title: Ethnobotany in five Shuar communities
sources.note: Contemporary multi-community study records plant knowledge and use while requiring caution about efficacy and historical projection.

sources.title: Medicinal plants in the Shimpis Shuar community
sources.note: University repository study documents local plant names, preparations and uses in a contemporary community.

sources.title: Growth, infection and household conditions among Shuar children
sources.note: Open peer-reviewed modern health study measures water, latrines and infection; used to show present variation and the historical evidence gap.

sources.title: Co-produced climate and ecological knowledge with Shuar communities
sources.note: Contemporary open research emphasizes community authority, gardens, fishing, cooking and plant knowledge in collaborative science.

sources.title: Authenticating a tsantsa with scientific and cultural evidence
sources.note: Heritage Science study combines imaging and provenance research while discussing colonial collecting, forgeries and repatriation.

sources.title: Micro-CT analysis of a tsantsa
sources.note: Open scientific study demonstrates imaging methods and ethical responsibilities toward human remains.

sources.title: Ethics and tsantsas
sources.note: Pitt Rivers Museum education page centers human-remains ethics, community consultation and colonial collecting.

sources.title: Circulation, accumulation and the power of Shuar shrunken heads
sources.note: Cultural Anthropology article traces changing meanings and the harmful effects of outside demand rather than treating tsantsa as a timeless spectacle.

proposedOverrides.summary: An evidence-aware guide to Shuar communities, language, households, environment, colonial resistance, daily life and living continuity across the atlas layer’s approximate 1279 to 1878 span.
